<design_philosophy>
You are building ONE web page whose only job is to let a reader understand a research paper faster
than they could by opening the PDF. Every decision on the page is judged against that.

WHAT "FASTER" MEANS HERE
- A reader who leaves after thirty seconds still knows the finding and the number behind it.
- A reader who stays five minutes has the method, the figures and the caveats, in that order.
- Nothing on the page is there because a layout had a slot for it.

ACCURACY IS THE HARD CONSTRAINT
Every number, name and claim comes from the paper as written — you read them out of the LaTeX
source, the only source this page has. You never change a number's precision, never restate a
comparison the paper did not make, and never invent a headline figure to fill a card. A page that
looks excellent and misreports one result is worse than no page, because the PDF beside it says
something else and a reader will find that out.

CRAFT, AND THE LOOK TO AVOID
The failure mode for a generated page is a look every reader now recognises on sight: a
purple-to-blue gradient banner, three identical cards with emoji headings, and body text set in
one weight at one size. Avoid all of it.
- Type carries the design. One system font stack, a real scale with visible jumps between levels
  rather than a creep of similar sizes, long-form text around 17-19px with a measure of 65-75
  characters and generous line height. Weight and size do the emphasis; colour rarely does.
- Colour is restrained. A light, near-white ground, one dark ink for text, one accent used for
  links and the current-section marker and almost nothing else. No gradients as decoration.
- Space does the work that borders and boxes would do badly. Sections separated by real vertical
  rhythm, cards defined by alignment and a single hairline rather than by shadow stacks.
- Structure over ornament: no emoji as section markers, no icon fonts, no badge clutter, no
  animated counters.
- Motion is a courtesy. A short transition on a lightbox or a hover state is welcome; anything
  that moves on scroll, autoplays, or delays the reader is not — and all of it stops under
  prefers-reduced-motion.
- Every interactive element works with a keyboard and says what it is to a screen reader. That is
  part of the craft, not a checklist bolted on at the end.

FINISH IT
The page is done when you have opened it in a browser, read it at a phone width and a desktop
width, tabbed through every control, and found nothing to fix. Not before.
</design_philosophy>

<page_structure>
In this order, top to bottom:

1. HERO — the paper's title, the author line as the paper gives it, and a one-paragraph TL;DR in
   plain language: what was asked, what was found, and the single number that carries the finding.
   Not the abstract, and not a rewrite of it. Below it, every link the links section below
   lists, each at the exact URL given there.
2. CONTRIBUTIONS — the paper's actual contributions as three to five scannable cards, each a short
   heading plus one or two sentences. If the paper claims four things, show four cards, not five.
3. METHOD — a walkthrough a technically literate non-specialist can follow: what goes in, what
   happens to it, what comes out, and why the design is the way it is. Lead with the paper's own
   method figure when it has one.
4. RESULTS — the paper's real headline numbers, read out of `paper.tex`, each next to what it was measured on and what it is being compared against.
   A number that is not in the paper does not go on the page, and neither does a comparison the
   paper did not make. If a slot has no number, drop the slot.
5. FIGURE GALLERY — every figure, each with its caption, click-to-enlarge into a lightbox that
   closes on Escape, on a click outside, and on a visible close control.
6. LIMITATIONS — what the paper says it does not show. Verbatim in substance; do not soften it.
7. FOOTER — every link from the links section again, and the citation if the paper carries one.

A sticky section navigation runs alongside all of it and marks where the reader currently is.
Do NOT write its highlighting yourself: hand-written ones kept a stale section lit after a jump
back to the top, or never reached the short last sections. Instead give the nav element a
`data-scrollspy` attribute, make each of its links `href="#<id of that section>"`, style the
current link through `a.active` (it also gets `aria-current`), and paste this script VERBATIM
into the page's script element at the end of the body. It lights the section in view, the last one once the page is
scrolled to its end, and nothing while the reader is above the first linked section:

```js
/* aii-scroll-spy v1: paste verbatim */
(function () {
  var links = [], targets = [];
  document.querySelectorAll('[data-scrollspy] a[href^="#"]').forEach(function (a) {
    var el = document.getElementById(a.getAttribute('href').slice(1));
    if (el) { links.push(a); targets.push(el); }
  });
  if (!links.length) return;
  var queued = false;
  function current() {
    var view = window.innerHeight;
    var doc = document.documentElement;
    var atEnd = window.scrollY > 0 && view + window.scrollY >= doc.scrollHeight - 2;
    var line = atEnd ? view - 1 : Math.min(view * 0.3, 200);
    var best = null, bestTop = -Infinity;
    targets.forEach(function (el) {
      var top = el.getBoundingClientRect().top;
      if (top <= line && top > bestTop) { best = el; bestTop = top; }
    });
    return best;
  }
  function update() {
    queued = false;
    var el = current();
    links.forEach(function (a, i) {
      var on = targets[i] === el;
      a.classList.toggle('active', on);
      if (on) a.setAttribute('aria-current', 'location');
      else a.removeAttribute('aria-current');
    });
  }
  function schedule() {
    if (!queued) { queued = true; window.requestAnimationFrame(update); }
  }
  window.addEventListener('scroll', schedule, { passive: true });
  window.addEventListener('resize', schedule);
  window.addEventListener('load', schedule);
  if (window.ResizeObserver) new ResizeObserver(schedule).observe(document.body);
  update();
})();
```
</page_structure>

<technical_requirements>
- ONE file. All CSS in a style element, all JavaScript in a script element, both inline in
  `index.html`. No build step, no bundler, no framework, no external script, stylesheet, web
  font or analytics — nothing fetched at load time. The page must render with the network off,
  and the only local files it may point at are the figures listed above; the PDF is linked at
  its full URL, never by its local name.
- A complete HTML document: the file opens with exactly this markup, then the title and the
  style element, and closes head before the body. The viewport tag is what makes a phone lay the
  page out at its own width; without it the page renders 980px wide and shrinks to tiny text.
```html
<!DOCTYPE html><html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"><meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
```
- System font stack only, since no font may be downloaded.
- Light theme. Responsive from a 360px phone to a wide desktop, with no horizontal page scroll;
  wide content scrolls inside its own container.
- Honour prefers-reduced-motion: under it, transitions and any scroll-driven effect stop.
- Keyboard-navigable: every control reachable by Tab in a sensible order, a visible focus ring,
  the lightbox trapping focus while open and returning it to the thumbnail on close, and a skip
  link to the main content.
- Semantic HTML: one top-level heading, headings that descend without skipping, landmark elements,
  and alt text on every image that says what the figure shows rather than repeating its number.
- No emoji anywhere. No purple-to-blue gradients. No decorative icon fonts.
- Keep the whole file comfortably under a megabyte.
</technical_requirements>

<writing_register>
Write in the register of the field's best papers (the paper this page presents, which was written to them), not in the register of a language
model. Four things are measured on the finished draft, and a draft outside them is sent back with
the numbers:
- Never use: delve, underscore, showcase, intricate, pivotal, realm, commendable, meticulous, tapestry, garner, multifaceted, it is worth noting, plays a crucial role, not only ... but also. These are 10 to 30 times more frequent in machine-written abstracts than in
  human ones, and reviewers read them as such.
- Em dashes: at most 3 per 1,000 words. Use a comma, a colon or a full stop.
- Sentence rhythm: mix short and long sentences. An interquartile range of sentence length under
  8 words reads as machine-written.
- Hedging: at most 15 hedges (may, likely, suggests, appears) per 1,000
  words. State what the evidence supports plainly; hedge where it is thin, not everywhere.
Style never changes substance: numbers, claims, citations and figure markers stay exactly as the
evidence gives them. The user's original request (delivered as a separate message) overrides all
of this wherever the two conflict.
</writing_register>

Concepts are noun-phrase surface forms that first appeared in\nOpenAlex~\\citep{Priem2022} titles and abstracts between 2005 and 2016, with 20 to 300 papers in the\nfirst-appearance window and no more than 8,000 total works through 2024.%\n\\footnote{Code: \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-1/dataset-1}.}\nOf the 426, 366 are main emerging concepts (247 Screen, 119 Held-out, split by a SHA-1 hash on concept\nidentifiers) and 60 are stationary reference concepts. A logistic-regression classifier trained on\nsilver-standard labels (F1 $= 0.82$ on 300 test items, AUC $= 0.89$) and a variant merger (B-cubed\nF1 $= 0.78$) were applied to ground every concept.%\n\\footnote{Code: \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-2/experiment-1}.}\nThe pool is dominated by physics, physical-sciences and computer-science concepts sourced from arXiv.\nFor the Screen fold, 202 concepts survive grounding filters; for the Held-out fold, 100.\n\n\\paragraph{MeSH check population.} An independent biomedical arm of 191 concepts was drawn from new MeSH\ndescriptors (DateEstablished 2006 to 2016, widened to 2004--2005 and 2017--2018), surviving a provenance\nfilter, a PubMed novelty pre-screen and the same early-volume rule. Only approximately 25\\% of new MeSH\ndescriptors are genuinely new concepts; the remainder are reclassifications or splits.\n\n\\paragraph{Works.} The combined corpus comprises 462,812 unique OpenAlex works with 488,078 verified\nconcept--work links, spanning 2000 to 2024.\n\n\\paragraph{Co-word network.} From a design-weighted whole-science background sample of 259,716 works, we\nbuilt 25 yearly three-year-window co-occurrence snapshots (approximately 27,000 nodes and 84,000 edges per\nsnapshot), with association-strength edge weights~\\citep{vanEck2009}, Leiden community\ndetection~\\citep{Traag2018} (best of five seeds) and alluvial community identifiers.%\n\\footnote{Code: \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-2/experiment-3}.}\n\n\\paragraph{Host-nativeness profiles.} For each concept-keyword node, we retrieved exact OpenAlex\nsubfield-by-time-block publication counts, covering 78.7\\% of host co-occurrence weight across 1,372 nodes.\nThese profiles supply the host-vocabulary share used in RQ2. Figure~\\ref{fig:network} shows a schematic of the\nresulting network.\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig2_v0.jpg}\n  \\caption{Schematic illustration of the co-word network structure. Nodes represent concept-keyword terms\n  and grey edges represent co-occurrence links; node fill colour marks Leiden community\n  membership, and larger circles are high-degree hub terms. Background terms (plain nodes) form dense\n  communities joined by a few inter-community edges. Pool concepts (bold black rings) sit on the periphery\n  of communities, mostly in the gaps between two of them, where they act as bridge or connector nodes; three\n  are labelled as examples (\\emph{wireless backhaul}, \\emph{EPR steering}, \\emph{holographic QCD}); their\n  placement in the diagram is illustrative and does not reflect their actual network coordinates. The full\n  network comprises approximately 27,000 nodes and 84,000 edges; the panel is a schematic rendering\n  for readability and does not depict a specific yearly snapshot.}\n  \\label{fig:network}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\subsection{Structural precursors of emergence}\n\\label{sec:rq1method}\n\n\\paragraph{Emergence labels.} The pre-declared emergence label required a concept-year reaching at least 20\npapers per year and gaining at least 20 percentile points in co-word network strength. Because pool concepts sit\nin the bottom few percent of network strength, it produced only 4 onsets, so a sustained-uptake label\n($E_{\\mathrm{up}}$) was promoted after that result was seen; $E_{\\mathrm{up}}$ is therefore a post-hoc label, and\nevery RQ1 result below uses it. Its held-out test was then specified and frozen before the held-out fold was\nopened.\n\n\\paragraph{Matched event study.} For each concept showing sustained uptake, we matched it to a control concept\nfrom the same first-appearance band and origin field that did not show sustained uptake, using 1:1\nnearest-neighbour matching on pre-period network indicators. The standardised mean difference between treated\nand control concepts at lags $k = -3$ to $0$ is the event-study estimand. A pooled panel regression of\nthe binary future-emergence indicator on the closure measure provides a second estimand, reported as the panel\ncoefficient. Bootstrap confidence intervals ($B = 2{,}000$) and Holm-corrected $p$-values control for multiple\ntesting. The Screen fold (202 concepts) produced 68 onsets and 26 matched pairs.\n\n\\paragraph{Closure measures.} To test whether pre-emergence closure is reducible to neighbourhood turnover\nor Burt brokerage, we computed four variants: (a) turnover-residualised closure, obtained by regressing\nclosure on the new-relation rate, novelty, Baselga beta-similarity, log volume, concept age and Shannon\nentropy; (b) persistent-neighbour closure, restricting the closure coefficient to the top-20 neighbours\npresent in both year $y$ and $y{-}1$; (c) Burt constraint and effective size of the weighted ego\nnetwork~\\citep{Burt2004}; and (d) cross-community pair excess, defined as the count of partner pairs from\ndistinct Leiden communities minus the count expected under a strength-decile null.\n\n\\subsection{Host-entry grafting}\n\\label{sec:rq2method}\n\n\\paragraph{Host-entry events.} A host-entry event is the first year in which a concept appears in a\nnon-origin subfield together with at least five co-occurring partner terms. From 4,177 main-arm host entries,\nthe Screen fold retains 1,544 events across 140 concept clusters after the partner-count filter.\n\n\\paragraph{Exposure variable.} Host-vocabulary share is the tag-weighted mean of each partner's pre-entry\npublication share in the host subfield, where tag-weighted means that each co-occurrence edge is weighted by\nits association strength. The continuous measure is primary because only 1.1\\% of partner tags have a host\nshare above 50\\%. Co-transfer is the fraction of partners that were origin companions of the concept in the\nfive years before entry.\n\n\\paragraph{Outcome.} Five-year newcomer uptake: the count of host-subfield papers by author-disjoint newcomers\n(authors with no prior concept paper and no co-authorship with concept authors) during the five years after entry.\n\n\\paragraph{Model.} Poisson pseudo-maximum-likelihood (PPML) regression~\\citep{Silva2006} with\nconcept-clustered standard errors~\\citep{Cameron2015}. Two specifications were pre-registered. The primary\nspecification includes concept-by-entry-year and host-by-entry-year fixed effects. The co-primary specification\nincludes concept, entry-year and host fixed effects; a pre-declared thin-cell rule makes it co-primary when the\nprimary specification retains less than 30\\% of events or fewer than 50 concept clusters, which happened on the\nScreen fold (the primary retained 26\\% of events, 77 clusters). Both specifications include co-transfer as a second\nregressor.\n\n\\paragraph{Held-out fold.} 93 concepts, 1,100 entries; minimum detectable effect (co-primary): IRR per\nstandard deviation of 1.15. Its entry events and pre-entry (W1) features were computed before any outcome was\nread, but its outcomes stayed sealed under a hash-checked specification until they were opened once, with a\nlock file, after the screen analysis was frozen.\n\n\\paragraph{MeSH replication.} The same analysis was applied to 191 MeSH concepts under a frozen specification.\nThe declared design (at least five partners and nativeness coverage of at least 0.50) yielded only 192 events in\n46 non-singleton concepts, so the pre-declared widening (at least three partners, coverage 0.30) fired before\noutcomes were read, producing 2,171 co-primary events across 160 concept clusters. Entries into non-biomedical\nhosts are dropped, so the replication covers biomedicine-to-biomedicine entries only.\n\n\\subsection{Post-confirmation decomposition}\n\\label{sec:decomposition}\n\nAfter the Held-out and MeSH tests confirmed the host-vocabulary effect, three decompositions were\nspecified and frozen before any coefficient was read; because every fold had already been opened, they are\npost-confirmation exploratory:\n\n\\begin{itemize}\n\\item \\textbf{Extensive versus intensive margins.} A linear probability model for whether any newcomer uptake\noccurs (extensive margin), and PPML conditional on uptake having started (intensive margin). Inverse-variance\nweighting (IVW) pools estimates across the Screen, Held-out and MeSH folds.\n\n\\item \\textbf{Host-specific versus generic accessibility.} Generality proxies (tag-weighted normalised subfield\nentropy and log block frequency of each partner) are added as controls. The Balassa-index lift\nmeasure~\\citep{Balassa1965}, defined as the log ratio of the host-vocabulary share to the partner's baseline\nsubfield share, is tested as an alternative exposure variable.\n\n\\item \\textbf{Origin-field dependence.} A Wald test of equality across origin-field groups (Physics and\nAstronomy, Computer Science, other).\n\\end{itemize}\n\n\\section{Results}\n\\label{sec:results}\n\n\\subsection{RQ1: Structural precursors of emergence}\n\\label{sec:rq1}\n\n\\subsubsection{Experimental setup}\n\\label{sec:rq1_setup}\n\nThe Screen fold (202 concepts) produced 68 onsets of sustained uptake and 26 matched concept pairs after 1:1\nnearest-neighbour matching on pre-period network indicators. The Held-out fold produced 30 onsets and 22\nmatched pairs; because the Held-out fold's own never-treated pool was too small (33 concepts), 17 of 25 unique\ncontrols were drawn from the Screen fold's never-treated pool, so the Held-out estimator is not fully\ncontrol-side independent.\n\n\\subsubsection{Results}\n\\label{sec:rq1_results}\n\nOn the Screen fold, concepts that later show sustained uptake have lower general closure in the years before\nonset (matched event-study standardised mean difference $= -0.44$, 95\\% CI $[-0.81, -0.05]$; panel\ncoefficient $= -0.66$). The pre-registered positive sign was not observed; the effect runs in the opposite\ndirection.\n\n\\begin{table}[!htbp]\n\\centering\n\\caption{Closure on the sealed held-out fold. ``Screen panel'' is the panel coefficient on\nthe Screen fold. ``HO panel'' and ``HO event-study'' are the panel coefficient and matched event-study\nstandardised mean difference on the Held-out fold. Holm-corrected $p$-values apply to the panel coefficient.}\n\\label{tab:closure}\n\\footnotesize\n\\begin{tabularx}{\\linewidth}{X c c c c l}\n\\toprule\nMeasure & Screen panel & HO panel & HO event-study [95\\% CI] & Holm $p$ & Status \\\\\n\\midrule\nGeneral closure & $-0.66$ & $-0.39$ & $-0.53\\;[-1.20, +0.07]$ & 0.147 & Not confirmed \\\\\nTurnover-resid. & $-0.40$ & $-0.11$ & $-0.27\\;[-0.89, +0.30]$ & 0.635 & Not confirmed \\\\\nPersistent-neighbour & $-1.12$ & $-1.07$ & $-0.83\\;[-1.71, -0.10]$ & 0.015 & Confirmed \\\\\nBurt constraint & $+0.06$ & $+0.08$ & $+0.11\\;[+0.02, +0.19]$ & --- & Positive \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\multicolumn{6}{l}{\\scriptsize HO = Held-out fold. Holm $p$ tests the panel coefficient.}\n\\end{tabularx}\n\\end{table}\n\nTable~\\ref{tab:closure} and Figure~\\ref{fig:closure} summarise these results. On the sealed held-out fold,\ngeneral closure is not significant (Holm $p = 0.147$), and the frozen kill mapping returns R1\\_DEAD:\nstructural precursors of sustained uptake are volume/churn correlates. Only persistent-neighbour closure, restricted to top-20 neighbours present in consecutive\nyears, is significant: the panel coefficient is $-1.07$ (Holm $p = 0.015$) and the matched event-study\nstandardised mean difference is $-0.83$ (95\\% CI $[-1.71, -0.10]$). Burt constraint has the same positive\nsign on the Held-out fold (event-study $+0.11$, 95\\% CI $[0.02, 0.19]$), indicating that the lower closure\nbefore emergence is not Burt brokerage: concepts that later emerge sit in ego networks that are more\nconstrained, not less (effective size is also lower on held-out, $-27.8$, 95\\% CI $[-49.3, -9.5]$). The\npersistent-neighbour row carries three caveats: its screen event-study interval included zero ($-0.58$,\n95\\% CI $[-1.27, 0.12]$), 17 of the 25 held-out controls are screen concepts, and covariate balance is poor\n(entropy standardised mean difference 0.96; 6 of 11 covariates above 0.25).\n\nThe MeSH replication is directional under a sensitivity label (standardised mean difference $D = -0.42$, Holm $p = 0.039$, $n = 29$),\nsame sign as the main pool, but under the primary label the MeSH effect is null ($D = -0.09$, Holm\n$p = 0.677$, $n = 15$).%\n\\footnote{Code: \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-2/experiment-4}.}\n\nStructural precursors add no predictive value for whether a concept will later show sustained uptake beyond\nfrequency, burst, degree and entropy baselines (logistic AUC 0.89 versus 0.88, delta $-0.010$, 95\\% CI\n$-0.045$ to 0.021).\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig3_v0.pdf}\n  \\caption{Pre-emergence closure on the held-out fold, by measure type. Each row shows the standardised mean\n  difference between concepts that later show sustained uptake and matched controls. Points are estimates\n  and horizontal bars are 95\\% bootstrap confidence intervals. The dashed vertical line marks no effect,\n  and Holm-corrected $p$-values are listed to the right of the first three rows. Only\n  persistent-neighbour closure (blue) survives Holm correction (event-study $-0.83$, 95\\% CI\n  $[-1.71, -0.10]$; panel coefficient $-1.07$, Holm $p = 0.015$). General closure\n  (Holm $p = 0.147$) and turnover-residualised closure (Holm $p = 0.635$) are shown in grey: they do not\n  survive confirmation, and their intervals cross zero. Burt constraint (orange) is positive ($+0.11$,\n  95\\% CI $[0.02, 0.19]$), which indicates that emerging concepts sit in more constrained, not more\n  brokered, ego networks.}\n  \\label{fig:closure}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\subsubsection{Comparison to related work}\n\\label{sec:rq1_comparison}\n\nThe finding that emerging concepts show lower closure among their most stable co-word neighbours is consistent\nwith the work of \\citet{Salatino2017}, who found that new topics tend to emerge where weakly interconnected\nresearch areas begin to cross-fertilise, and with \\citeauthor{Chen2009}'s~\\citeyearpar{Chen2009} theory of structural variation\nin which transformative work bridges structural holes. It is also consistent with the structural-holes\nliterature~\\citep{Burt2004}: concepts that later emerge connect across Leiden communities, and their\ncross-community pair excess is positive. The critical difference is that Burt constraint is higher, not lower.\nIn Burt's framework, brokerage means low constraint. Here the ego network is more redundant, not less, so an\nincreasing-brokerage pathway is ruled out for these concepts. The pre-registered reading that openness is\nconfined to the top of an otherwise dense neighbourhood was tested on held-out and is not supported, because\nthe closure component was not confirmed. This pattern is\ncloser to what \\citet{Lin2022} describe as disconnection and discordance enabling new directions in science,\nand to \\citeauthor{Larson2017}'s~\\citeyearpar{Larson2017} finding that weak-tie diffusion in networks is not\nguaranteed to carry novel information.\n\nAmong Applied Network Science contributions, \\citet{Domenico2016} studied knowledge diaspora through\nsource-sink author flows, and \\citet{Cunningham2022} built field-of-study networks that link topics through the\nauthors who publish in them and used structural role analysis to characterise the multidisciplinary roles of\ntopics. Our analysis works at the level of concept co-word neighbourhoods rather than author-defined topic\nnetworks. \\citet{Fontaine2024} traced the penetration of AI into neuroscience and found epistemic integration\nalongside social segregation: AI research formed a distinct, socially confined ecosystem inside the field, a\ncase of presence in a field that differs from integration into it. \\citet{Doonan2019} found that community structure in co-inventor networks affects\ntime to first citation, paralleling our finding that community position shapes concept uptake.\n\n\\subsubsection{Discussion}\n\\label{sec:rq1_discussion}\n\nUnder the pre-registered kill rule, RQ1 is answered negatively: structural precursors of sustained uptake are\nvolume/churn correlates, and they add nothing to frequency, burst, degree and entropy baselines in prediction.\nThe qualification is the persistent-neighbour closure row: concepts whose top associates do not close into\ntriads from year to year are more likely to show sustained uptake on the held-out fold. It is a single row,\nits screen event-study interval included zero, and the held-out matching falls back to Screen controls for\n17 of 25 unique controls, so we treat it as a lead rather than a finding. Burt constraint is positive, meaning\nthe ego network is redundant, not brokered; brokerage across a structural hole is ruled out as the pathway.\n\n\\subsection{RQ2: Host-entry grafting}\n\\label{sec:rq2}\n\n\\subsubsection{Experimental setup}\n\\label{sec:rq2_setup}\n\nThe host-entry sample for the Screen fold comprises 1,544 events across 140 concept clusters (co-primary\nspecification). Entry is predominantly a package: 70\\% of partner tags are non-native origin companions, and\nonly 1.8\\% are native grafts (host share above 50\\%). The mean host-vocabulary share is 0.043 (SD 0.055). The\nHeld-out fold has 972 events across 74 concept clusters. The MeSH population has 2,171 events across 160\nconcept clusters.\n\n\\subsubsection{Results}\n\\label{sec:rq2_results}\n\n\\begin{table}[!htbp]\n\\centering\n\\caption{Host-entry grafting: pre-registered test. IRR/SD = incidence-rate ratio per one standard deviation\nof host-vocabulary share. CT = co-transfer. G = concept clusters. IVW = inverse-variance weighted pool of the Screen and MeSH\nco-primary estimates. The Screen primary row has Holm $p = 0.15$.}\n\\label{tab:grafting}\n\\small\n\\begin{tabularx}{\\linewidth}{l l c c c c c c}\n\\toprule\nSpecification & Fold & IRR/SD & 95\\% CI & $p$ & CT $p$ & $N$ & $G$ \\\\\n\\midrule\nCo-primary & Screen & 1.30 & 1.16--1.45 & ${<}\\,0.001$ & 0.48 & 1,544 & 140 \\\\\nCo-primary & Held-out & 1.19 & 1.06--1.33 & 0.004 & 0.60 & 972 & 74 \\\\\nPrimary (strict FE) & Held-out & 0.98 & 0.70--1.37 & 0.91 & 0.22 & 250 & 30 \\\\\nCo-primary & MeSH & 1.23 & 1.12--1.36 & ${<}\\,0.001$ & 0.053 & 2,171 & 160 \\\\\nPrimary & MeSH & 1.32 & 1.10--1.60 & 0.004 & 0.46 & 1,004 & 122 \\\\\nPrimary (strict FE) & Screen & 1.39 & 0.97--1.99 & 0.074 & 0.85 & 452 & 77 \\\\\nCo-primary (IVW) & Screen + MeSH & 1.26 & 1.17--1.36 & ${<}\\,0.001$ & --- & --- & --- \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabularx}\n\\end{table}\n\nTable~\\ref{tab:grafting} presents the pre-registered test. On the Screen fold, a one-standard-deviation\nincrease in host-vocabulary share raises newcomer uptake by 30\\% (co-primary IRR 1.30, 95\\% CI 1.16 to 1.45).\nOn the sealed held-out fold, opened once, the co-primary IRR is 1.19 (95\\% CI 1.06 to 1.33; Holm $p = 0.009$,\nwild-cluster bootstrap $p = 0.012$, nativeness-permutation $p = 0.026$, placebo-calibrated $p = 0.034$;\na within-concept shuffle permutation gives a borderline $p = 0.050$), so the pre-declared kill rule is not\ntriggered. Heterogeneity between Screen and Held-out is not significant ($p = 0.25$). On the MeSH biomedical\npopulation the co-primary IRR is 1.23 (95\\% CI 1.12 to 1.36, $p < 0.001$; primary IRR 1.32, 95\\% CI 1.10 to\n1.60, $p = 0.004$; pre-registered verdict: REPLICATED for biomedicine-to-biomedicine entries). The\ninverse-variance weighted pool of the Screen and MeSH co-primary estimates is 1.26 (95\\% CI 1.17\nto 1.36, $I^2 = 0$). Co-transfer is null across all folds and specifications\n(Figure~\\ref{fig:grafting}).\n\nThe fully saturated primary specification on the Held-out fold is inconclusive (IRR 0.98, 95\\% CI 0.70 to\n1.37) because it retains only 250 of 972 events with 30 concept clusters; this was declared underpowered in\nadvance (minimum detectable effect IRR 1.30).\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig4_v0.pdf}\n  \\caption{Host-vocabulary effect on five-year newcomer uptake across folds and specifications. Each row gives\n  the PPML incidence-rate ratio (IRR) per one standard deviation of host-vocabulary share, on a log axis;\n  horizontal bars are 95\\% concept-clustered confidence intervals, and the dashed vertical line marks\n  IRR $= 1$ (no effect). Filled circles are the co-primary specification (concept, entry-year and host fixed\n  effects) and open circles the primary specification with concept$\\times$year and host$\\times$year fixed\n  effects. Blue marks the OpenAlex screen and sealed held-out folds, green the independent MeSH replication,\n  and the amber diamond the inverse-variance weighted (IVW) pooled co-primary estimate. The co-primary effect\n  is significant on all three folds (screen IRR 1.30 [1.16, 1.45], held-out 1.19 [1.06, 1.33], MeSH 1.23\n  [1.12, 1.36]), and the pooled estimate is 1.26 [1.17, 1.36] (Screen and MeSH co-primary). The primary specification is inconclusive on\n  the held-out fold (IRR 0.98 [0.70, 1.37], 30 clusters, $p = 0.91$) but significant on MeSH (IRR 1.32\n  [1.10, 1.60]). Grey diamonds are the co-transfer regressor from the co-primary models. Its intervals\n  include 1 on every fold ($p = 0.48$, $0.60$ and $0.053$). The right-hand columns list each estimate with\n  its 95\\% CI and $p$-value.}\n  \\label{fig:grafting}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\paragraph{Robustness.} The co-primary effect holds in 20 of 26 robustness variants on the Screen fold\nincluding the base row and field strata, and in 18 of 22 excluding them (IRR range 1.11 to 1.56 among\nsignificant rows); binary nativeness cut-offs at 0.5 and 0.7 are null. All seven pre-specified robustness rows on the Held-out fold are\nsignificant. Nativeness-permutation placebos are centred on 1.0 (co-primary $p = 0.002$ Screen, 0.026\nHeld-out, 0.010 MeSH). The cluster-robust variance estimator mildly over-rejects at the null (size 10.5\\% on\nMeSH simulation), so $p$-values should be read alongside the wild-cluster and permutation results.\n\n\\subsubsection{Mechanism decomposition}\n\\label{sec:rq2_mechanism}\n\n\\paragraph{Extensive versus intensive margins.} The host-vocabulary effect operates through both the extensive\nmargin, meaning whether any newcomer uptake starts, and the intensive margin, meaning the count of newcomer\npapers given that uptake started. The inverse-variance weighted extensive-margin effect is $+6.4$ percentage\npoints per standard deviation (95\\% CI 4.8 to 8.1, randomisation-$t$ $p < 0.001$), approximately a 13\\%\nincrease relative to the base rate of 51\\%. The inverse-variance weighted intensive-margin incidence-rate ratio\nper standard deviation is 1.18 (95\\% CI 1.10 to 1.27). The extensive share of the total effect is 0.38\n(95\\% CI 0.21 to 0.55; Figure~\\ref{fig:margins}).\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig5_v0.pdf}\n  \\caption{Decomposition of the host-vocabulary effect into extensive and intensive margins across the screen,\n  held-out and MeSH folds. Blue circles show per-fold estimates, vermillion diamonds the inverse-variance-weighted\n  (IVW) pooled estimate, and horizontal bars 95\\% confidence intervals. (a)~Extensive margin:\n  linear-probability-model effect of a one-standard-deviation increase in host-vocabulary share on the\n  probability of any newcomer uptake, in percentage points per SD (dashed line: no effect). The pooled effect\n  is 6.43~pp (95\\% CI 4.76 to 8.11). (b)~Intensive margin: PPML incidence-rate ratio per SD conditional on\n  uptake, on a log axis (dashed line: IRR $= 1$). The pooled IRR is 1.183 (95\\% CI 1.104 to 1.267). All three\n  folds are positive on both margins, and every fold interval excludes the null. (c)~Share of the total effect:\n  the extensive margin accounts for 38\\% (95\\% CI 21\\% to 55\\%, black whisker) and the intensive margin for\n  the remaining 62\\%.}\n  \\label{fig:margins}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\paragraph{Host-specific versus generic accessibility.} Adding generality controls (subfield entropy and log\nfrequency of entry partners) to the co-primary model retains 97\\% of the host-vocabulary coefficient\n(inverse-variance weighted retention 0.97, 95\\% CI 0.81 to 1.10), and the Balassa-index lift measure is also\nsignificant (inverse-variance weighted IRR per standard deviation 1.34, 95\\% CI 1.23 to 1.46). The\nhost-vocabulary gradient is not reducible to generic concept accessibility. However, within fixed effects the\nBalassa-index lift measure has a correlation of 0.997 with the log of the continuous host-vocabulary share,\nso the lift leg of this test is weak: the two measures carry nearly the same within-unit information, and the\nlift result should be interpreted as confirming the continuous share rather than adding independent evidence\nfor host-specificity.\n\n\\paragraph{No origin-field boundary.} The Wald test for equality of the host-vocabulary effect across\norigin-field groups (Physics and Astronomy, Computer Science, other) is null ($p = 0.64$, label-permutation\n$p = 0.77$). Physics and Astronomy concepts, whose host-vocabulary coefficient is individually non-significant\n(IRR 1.18, 95\\% CI 0.93 to 1.50), fall within sampling variation of the other groups.\n\n\\subsubsection{Diffusion typology and expansion-before-diffusion ordering}\n\\label{sec:rq2_typology}\n\nA data-derived typology based on multivariate dynamic time warping of three diversity channels (rarefied\nShannon entropy, Rao-Stirling diversity~\\citep{Stirling2007} and active subfield count) yields a stable\ntwo-cluster solution ($k$-medoids, Hennig bootstrap~\\citep{Hennig2007} minimum Jaccard 0.86):\n\\textbf{localised} ($n = 136$, low entropy and few active subfields) and \\textbf{broad from the start}\n($n = 66$, high entropy from early years). Finer clusterings are unstable ($k = 3$ Jaccard 0.60). The typology\ndoes not separate outcomes better than an entropy-only baseline after residualising on early volume.\n\nCrossing the typology with rooting separates occupancy from rooting. On the Screen fold, broad-from-the-start\nconcepts have almost three times as many host entries per concept as localised ones (18.4 versus 6.6) and a\nhigher establishment rate (0.31 versus 0.13). Their raw host-vocabulary share is lower, and after host-by-year\nfixed effects and relatedness density the gap is null on both folds (Screen $-0.0018$; Held-out $+0.0005$,\n95\\% CI $-0.010$ to 0.011), so the pre-declared prediction that broad concepts arrive with more host vocabulary\nfails. Their co-transfer is lower (Held-out $-0.125$, 95\\% CI $-0.19$ to $-0.06$): broadly integrated concepts\ntravel less as packages. Within each type, host-vocabulary share predicts newcomer uptake (Screen PPML IRR per SD\n1.36 for broad and 1.16 for localised concepts; interaction $p = 0.11$, exploratory). The typology measures where\na concept is present; host-vocabulary share measures whether it is taken up there.\n\nAmong concepts exhibiting both a co-word-network expansion onset and a disciplinary-diffusion onset, expansion\nprecedes diffusion in 25 of 26 pooled main-arm cases (proportion 0.96, bootstrap 95\\% CI 0.88 to 1.00; on the\nScreen fold alone 15 of 16 against a year-shuffle null of 0.62, $p = 0.004$), but only 8.6\\% of concepts have\nboth onsets observable. This ordering holds only conditionally: diffusion onsets are rarer overall (log-rank\n$p = 0.005$), the evaluability rule favours this order, the cohort first seen by 2012 has only 12 dual-onset\nconcepts, and the Granger panel coefficient is negative and not significant ($b = -0.0013$, $p = 0.068$). On\nMeSH, 9 of 13 show expansion first (not different from the null, $p = 0.43$).\n\n\\subsubsection{Adopter-level mechanism}\n\\label{sec:rq2_adopter}\n\nAdopters, defined as author-disjoint newcomers who publish a concept paper in the host subfield within the\nfive-year outcome window, are more likely to have prior corpus exposure to the concept's entry partners than matched non-adopters\nfrom the same host subfield (conditional logistic regression: OR 3.09; prevalence 0.79 versus 0.61; 95\\% CI\n2.32 to 4.28; 1,013 matched strata, 422 entries, 109 concepts). Exposure to frequency-matched\nnegative-control concepts is negatively associated (OR 0.62), and the placebo control using partners of a\ndifferent concept's entry into the same host is also below 1 (OR 0.72), showing specificity to the concept's\nown partners. Exposure is measured only within the corpus: 87\\% of the 21,941 adopter pairs have no prior corpus\nwork and are excluded.\n\nDecomposing partners into three vocabulary classes --- FOREIGN (origin vocabulary, host share below 5\\%),\nADJACENT (5\\% to 30\\%) and NATIVE (host vocabulary, above 30\\%) --- enrichment follows a gradient: FOREIGN\npartners OR 2.88, ADJACENT partners OR 1.91, NATIVE partners OR 1.47. Adopters who pick up a concept in a new\nfield are most enriched for prior exposure to its origin-vocabulary partners. This is consistent with the\nabsorptive-capacity framework~\\citep{Cohen1990}, in which recognising external knowledge depends on prior\nfamiliarity with it, and equally with plain topical proximity of adopters to the concept. Enrichment does not\ninteract with host-vocabulary share (OR 0.87, 95\\% CI 0.70 to 1.14), and the pre-exposed adopter pool does not\nmediate the entry-level effect (attenuation 0.05, 95\\% CI $-0.08$ to 0.23). This Screen-fold result is not\nindependently confirmed.\n\n\\subsubsection{Representative cases}\n\\label{sec:rq2_cases}\n\nFour medoid cases from the typology clusters illustrate the host-vocabulary gradient at the concept level\n(Figure~\\ref{fig:cases}).\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig6_v0.pdf}\n  \\caption{Four representative cases of the host-vocabulary gradient. Each panel shows one concept, and each\n  horizontal bar is one of its host entries in the co-primary sample, labelled by host subfield and entry year\n  and sorted by host-vocabulary share (x-axis, fraction). Green bars are rooted entries and grey bars are\n  non-rooted entries. The dashed line marks the mean share of the non-rooted entries, and rooted bars are\n  annotated with their share and number of newcomer papers. (a)~Wireless backhaul (broad, CS): 14 entries, one\n  rooted (Aerospace Engineering 2008, share 0.084, 6 newcomers) against a non-rooted mean of 0.021.\n  (b)~Einstein--Podolsky--Rosen (EPR) steering (broad, Physics): 7 entries, one rooted (Artificial Intelligence\n  2011, 0.142, 37 newcomers; co-transfer 0) against a non-rooted mean of 0.027. (c)~Locally repairable code\n  (localised, CS): a single co-primary entry, rooted (0.056, 3 newcomers), so there is no within-concept\n  contrast. (d)~Holographic QCD (localised, Physics): 5 entries, none rooted (mean 0.041; three have\n  co-transfer 1.0), including an AMO Physics entry at 0.132 that did not take root. In (a) and (b), the rooted\n  entry has a higher host-vocabulary share than every non-rooted entry of the same concept. The panels are\n  descriptive, so no intervals are drawn.}\n  \\label{fig:cases}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\paragraph{Wireless backhaul} (broad type, Computer Science, first appeared 2006). Broad from its first year,\nsplitting between Computer Networks and Electrical Engineering. By 2022 seven subfields are active. Of 14 host\nentries in the co-primary sample, only one is rooted (Aerospace Engineering in 2008, host-vocabulary share\n0.084, 6 newcomer papers). The 13 non-rooted entries average a host-vocabulary share of 0.021 and arrive as\norigin packages (co-transfer 0.6 to 1.0). Rooted-minus-unrooted host-vocabulary share: $+0.062$.\n\n\\paragraph{Einstein--Podolsky--Rosen steering} (broad type, Physics, first appeared 2011). Of 7 co-primary\nentries, one is rooted. The rooted entry's host subfield is labelled ``Artificial Intelligence'' in the\nOpenAlex subfield taxonomy; this placement arises because OpenAlex files the topic ``Quantum Information\nand Cryptography'' under its Artificial Intelligence subfield, which is broader than the colloquial meaning\nof AI. The rooted entry has host-vocabulary share 0.142, co-transfer 0,\nand 37 newcomer papers. The 6 non-rooted entries average 0.027 with co-transfer at or above 0.55.\nRooted-minus-unrooted: $+0.115$. A broad-type label can hide a concept whose cross-disciplinary integration\nrests on a single well-anchored entry.\n\n\\paragraph{Locally repairable code} (localised type, Computer Science, first appeared 2013). Stays at 84\\% to\n96\\% in Computer Networks for its life. Has only 1 co-primary entry. The host subfield for this entry is\nlabelled ``Artificial Intelligence'' in the OpenAlex taxonomy, because OpenAlex files the relevant topic under\nits AI subfield, following the same broad assignment noted above.\nHost-vocabulary share 0.056, rooted. Demonstrates rooting without broad occupancy.\n\n\\paragraph{Holographic QCD} (localised type, Physics, first appeared 2006). Stays at 95\\% to 97\\% in Nuclear\nand High Energy Physics. Its 5 co-primary entries are all non-rooted, averaging 0.041, with three having\nco-transfer of 1.0: pure origin packages. No entry is rooted. A locally concentrated concept whose excursions\nare packaged imports that do not take root.\n\n\\subsubsection{Comparison to related work}\n\\label{sec:rq2_comparison}\n\nOur host-vocabulary measure is closest to the ideational embeddedness of \\citet{Cheng2023}, who found that a\nconcept's fit with existing traditions raises its yearly article count. Their measure is a global property of\nthe concept (mean cosine similarity of all its neighbours in a word2vec embedding), whereas ours is\nentry-specific: measured at the level of each concept-subfield-year event, with concept and host fixed effects\nabsorbing concept-level confounds. Co-transfer, the natural competitor, is null. This extends the principle\nthat relatedness predicts diversification, documented in economic\ngeography~\\citep{Boschma2014, Hidalgo2018}, to the level of individual concept-entry events.\n\nAmong Applied Network Science papers, our work engages most directly with the source-sink analysis of\nknowledge diaspora by \\citet{Domenico2016}, which modelled author flows as diffusion on a bipartite field\nnetwork. Our approach measures concept-vocabulary composition at the entry point rather than author flows; we do\nnot compare the two channels. \\citet{Cunningham2022} characterised the multidisciplinary roles of topics in\nauthor-defined field-of-study networks. \\citet{Fontaine2024} found that AI entered neuroscience epistemically\nwhile its practitioners stayed socially segregated; our distinction between occupying a subfield and being\ntaken up by its own newcomers is in the same spirit. \\citet{Holmgren2023} developed multilevel alluvial methods for mapping\nchange in higher-order networks, related to the alluvial community tracking we use. \\citet{Medeuov2021}\ncompared semantic networks through concept-centred ego subnetworks, the same ego-level view that underlies our\nclosure and constraint measures.\n\\citet{Larson2017} showed that weak ties do not guarantee novel information diffusion, complementing our\nfinding that the vocabulary composition of entry partners, not merely the structural position, predicts rooting.\n\\citet{Doonan2019} found that co-inventor community structure affects time to first citation, providing\na parallel at the patent level to our concept-uptake results. \\citet{Cai2025} examined how knowledge-graph\nextraction errors propagate into downstream network analyses, an issue relevant to the OpenAlex concept\nassignments on which our co-word network is built.\n\n\\subsubsection{Discussion}\n\\label{sec:rq2_discussion}\n\nThe central finding is that a concept's first partners in a new subfield carry information about whether that\nconcept will subsequently be adopted by newcomer scientists in the host field. The host-vocabulary share\npredicts five-year newcomer uptake in a pre-registered design, confirmed on a sealed held-out fold and\nreplicated for biomedicine-to-biomedicine entries in a MeSH population. The effect is graded and on the count\nof newcomer papers; it does not predict a binary establishment threshold on the held-out fold.\n\nThe entry-level and adopter-level results are two separate channels, and we do not merge them into one\nmechanism. At the entry level, host-leaning vocabulary goes with more newcomer uptake. At the adopter level, the\nindividuals who pick up the concept are enriched for prior exposure to the concept's origin-vocabulary partners\n(OR 3.09; prevalence 0.79 vs.\\ 0.61; Screen fold, not independently confirmed), which is consistent with\nabsorptive capacity~\\citep{Cohen1990} or with topical proximity. Host-leaning entries do not raise uptake by\nenlarging this pre-exposed pool: the pool does not mediate the entry-level effect.\n\n\\subsection{Community roles and bridging}\n\\label{sec:community}\n\nLeiden community roles (five-seed agreement 97.2\\%) partition concepts into four categories: bridge (0.61),\nother (0.33), stayer (0.03) and migrant (0.02). Emerging concepts are peripheral or connector nodes in the\nGuimera--Amaral cartography~\\citep{Guimera2005a} (peripheral 0.49, connector 0.40, kinless 0.10, no hubs).\nLagged roles do not robustly predict host-subfield entry (bridge odds ratio 0.64, 95\\% CI 0.38 to 1.08).\n\nMost emerging concepts act as bridges between Leiden communities in the co-word network (early-bridging share\n0.70 in the main pool versus 0.59 in MeSH, difference $+0.11$, 95\\% CI 0.02 to 0.20), but this bridging role\nis common and non-discriminating.\n\n\\section{Discussion}\n\\label{sec:discussion}\n\n\\subsection{Null findings and what they bound}\n\nFigure~\\ref{fig:decision} places every test on the pre-registered decision path, with failed gates and null or\ndead tests kept in grey rather than dropped. Several pre-registered hypotheses were not supported. Co-transfer, defined as arriving with origin companions,\nis null in all specifications and populations, meaning that the composition of entry matters but the\nimported-package channel does not. The breadth-prediction screen (does openness predict how many new subfields\na concept will reach?) found no effect beyond growth and level baselines.%\n\\footnote{Code: \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-3/experiment-6}.}\nThe link between pre-emergence closure and later host-entry composition is null (partial correlation 0.025\nScreen, 0.053 Held-out, both confidence intervals including zero), meaning that network openness and vocabulary\ncomposition operate independently rather than through a shared mechanism.\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=0.88\\linewidth,height=0.66\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig7_v0.pdf}\n  \\caption{Population flow and pre-registered decision path (layout and numbers from the run's figure registry). (1)~Data and\n  grounding: 426 candidate concepts (366 emerging, 60 reference), 462,812 works, the sealed fold split (screen 202\n  and held-out 100 main concepts) and the 191-concept MeSH pool. (2)~The two network views. (3)~Decision path:\n  the source-sink viability hypothesis and Gate~A failed, so the pre-declared host-entry grafting test took over;\n  it was screened (1,544 events, 140 concepts), confirmed on the sealed held-out fold (972 events, 74 concepts) and\n  replicated in MeSH for biomedicine-to-biomedicine entries (2,171 events, 160 concepts), and the adopter test is\n  mechanism evidence on the screen fold. Grey dashed boxes are dead or null: openness predicting breadth, co-transfer,\n  the link from early closure to later host-vocabulary share, and RQ1 structural precursors, which the\n  held-out test declared dead. (4)~The RQ2 descriptive layer (the lead-lag share shown is the screen fold's 15 of\n  16). Construct definitions are given in Section~\\ref{sec:methods}.}\n  \\label{fig:decision}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\subsection{Limitations}\n\\label{sec:limitations}\n\n\\paragraph{What the held-out fold does and does not protect.} The held-out fold's outcomes were sealed and\nopened once, but its entry events, pre-entry features and population size were computed on the same pipeline\nbefore opening, and an early experiment computed origin-series summaries for 61 of its concepts. The\nconfirmation therefore guards against outcome-driven choices, not against every choice of frame. The MeSH\npopulation is not wholly unseen either: it was used for the RQ1 replication before the grafting test.\n\n\\paragraph{Population bias.} The concept pool is dominated by physics, physical-sciences and computer-science\nconcepts from arXiv. The MeSH population covers only biomedicine-to-biomedicine entries; its coverage rule removes 34\\% of\npartner-qualified entries, and PubMed-only entry years match all-works entry years for 50\\% of entries on the\n13 fully retrieved concepts. Generalisation to social sciences, humanities or engineering is untested.\n\n\\paragraph{Primary specification underpowered.} The fully saturated specification with concept-by-year and\nhost-by-year fixed effects, which absorbs more confounding than the co-primary, is inconclusive on the Held-out\nfold (IRR 0.98, 30 clusters). The held-out confirmation rests on the co-primary specification, which leaves\nmore residual variation; on MeSH the primary specification is significant (IRR 1.32).\n\n\\paragraph{Single-paper entries.} 87\\% of co-primary Screen events involve a single entry-year paper. The\npooled multi-team effect is positive (IRR 1.28, 95\\% CI 1.11 to 1.48), but the Held-out alone is underpowered\nfor this test.\n\n\\paragraph{Binary establishment null.} The host-vocabulary share predicts the count of newcomer papers and the\nprobability that any newcomer uptake occurs, but binary establishment (at least three newcomer papers, with host papers in at least\nthree of the five years) is null on the Held-out fold ($p = 0.165$). The effect is graded, not threshold-based.\n\n\\paragraph{Cluster-robust inference.} The cluster-robust variance estimator rejects 10\\% to 11\\% of null\nshuffles in simulation (target 5\\%; an earlier 200-draw audit reported 17.5\\%). Wild-cluster bootstrap and permutation tests give consistent results\n(Held-out wild $p = 0.012$, permutation $p = 0.026$), but the standard $p$-values should not be taken at\nface value.\n\n\\paragraph{Host-specificity caveat.} The Balassa-index lift measure used to test host-specificity has a\nwithin-fixed-effect correlation of 0.997 with the log of the continuous host-vocabulary share. The lift test\nconfirms the continuous measure rather than providing independent evidence.\n\n\\paragraph{Screen-fold adopter evidence.} The adopter-level enrichment (OR 3.09) is Screen-fold only, not\nindependently confirmed. The design cannot separate absorptive capacity from topical proximity.\n\n\\paragraph{Closure held-out caveats.} RQ1 is R1\\_DEAD under the frozen kill rule. The one confirmed row,\npersistent-neighbour closure, had a screen event-study interval that included zero, and the held-out matching\nfalls back to Screen controls for 17 of 25 unique controls, so the estimator is not fully control-side\nindependent; covariate balance is poor. The MeSH closure result is\ndirectional under the sensitivity label but null under the primary label.\n\n\\section{Conclusions}\n\\label{sec:conclusions}\n\nWhen a new scientific concept enters a disciplinary subfield, the vocabulary composition of its initial\npartners predicts whether newcomer scientists in that field will subsequently adopt it. This host-vocabulary\neffect (Screen IRR 1.30; sealed held-out IRR 1.19; MeSH co-primary IRR 1.23, verdict REPLICATED for\nbiomedicine-to-biomedicine entries) governs how much newcomer uptake follows rather than whether a binary\nestablishment threshold is crossed. It is host-specific\n--- though the Balassa-index lift leg of this test is near-collinear with the continuous share\n(within-fixed-effect $r = 0.997$) --- operates through both the extensive and intensive margins, and does\nnot vary by the concept's origin field. Co-transfer of origin companions is null.\n\nFor emergence, the answer is negative: structural precursors of sustained uptake are volume/churn\ncorrelates (R1\\_DEAD under the frozen kill rule). Persistent-neighbour closure is lower before sustained uptake on\nthe held-out fold (panel coefficient $-1.07$, Holm $p = 0.015$; event-study standardised mean difference\n$-0.83$, 95\\% CI $[-1.71, -0.10]$), but it is a single qualified row. Burt constraint is higher, so the\nincreasing-brokerage pathway is ruled out for emerging concepts.\n\nThese results bear on how knowledge transfer is evaluated and supported. Policies and platforms that facilitate\ncross-disciplinary research might benefit from attending to the vocabulary composition of a concept's first\nappearance in a new field, rather than only to the mobility of authors who carry it.\n\nFuture work should extend the concept pool beyond the physical and computational sciences, test whether the\nhost-vocabulary gradient holds for social-science and humanities concepts, and design an experiment to separate\nabsorptive capacity from topical proximity at the adopter level.\n\n\\section*{Declarations}\n\n\\paragraph{Availability of data and materials.} All data derive from OpenAlex, an open scholarly metadata\nindex. The concept pool, verified work lists and analysis code are available in the project repository at\n\\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new}.\n\n\\paragraph{Competing interests.} No competing interests are declared.\n\n\\paragraph{Funding.} Not applicable.\n\n\\paragraph{Authors' contributions.} Not applicable.\n\n\\bibliographystyle{plainnat}\n\\bibliography{references}\n\n\\end{document}\n", "numLines": 808, "startLine": 1, "totalLines": 808}}

<!-- HERO -->
<section id="hero" aria-label="Overview">
<h1>Host vocabulary predicts whether new scientific concepts take root across disciplinary boundaries</h1>

<p class="tldr">When a scientific concept first appears in a new disciplinary subfield, what determines whether it catches on? This study finds that the vocabulary composition of the concept's initial partner terms carries a signal: if those partners belong to the host field's own vocabulary, newcomer scientists in that field are substantially more likely to adopt the concept. A one-standard-deviation increase in host-vocabulary share raises five-year newcomer uptake by 26% (pooled incidence-rate ratio 1.26, 95% CI 1.17 to 1.36), confirmed on a sealed held-out fold and replicated independently in a biomedical population of 191 MeSH concepts.</p>

<div class="links-row">
  <a href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new@fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/paper.pdf">Read the paper (PDF)</a>
  <a href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new@fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/report.pdf">Read the full research report</a>
  <a href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new@fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/exec_summary.pdf">Read the executive summary</a>
  <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA">Code repository</a>
</div>

  <a href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new@fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-2/report.pdf">Round 2</a>,
  <a href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new@fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-3/report.pdf">Round 3</a>,
  <a href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new@fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-4/report.pdf">Round 4</a>,
  <a href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new@fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-5/report.pdf">Round 5</a>
</p>
</section>

<!-- CONTRIBUTIONS -->
<section id="contributions" aria-label="Contributions">
<h2>Contributions</h2>
<ol class="cards">

<li>
  <div class="card-head"><span class="card-num">1</span><h3>Host-vocabulary composition predicts newcomer uptake</h3></div>
  <div class="card-body">
    <p>A one-standard-deviation increase in host-vocabulary share raises five-year newcomer uptake by 30% on the screen fold (IRR 1.30, 95% CI 1.16 to 1.45), by 19% on a sealed <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-4/evaluation-2">held-out fold</a> opened once (IRR 1.19, 1.06 to 1.33), and by 23% in an independent <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-4/experiment-9">MeSH biomedical population</a> (IRR 1.23, 1.12 to 1.36; verdict REPLICATED for biomedicine-to-biomedicine entries).</p>
    <p class="code-links">Code: <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-3/experiment-7">Do borrowed ideas stick when grafted locally?</a></p>
  </div>
</li>

<li>
  <div class="card-head"><span class="card-num">2</span><h3>Outcome-blind, multi-population dataset</h3></div>
  <div class="card-body">
    <p><a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-2/dataset-5">426 OpenAlex concepts</a> (366 emerging, 60 stationary reference) with 462,812 works, split into screen and held-out folds, plus an independent <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-1/dataset-3">191-concept MeSH biomedical check population</a>.</p>
  </div>
</li>

<li>
  <div class="card-head"><span class="card-num">3</span><h3>Host-specific effect through both margins</h3></div>
  <div class="card-body">
    <p>The effect is host-specific (though the Balassa-index lift test is near-collinear with the continuous share), operates through both the <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-5/evaluation-6">extensive margin</a> (whether uptake starts: +6.4 pp per SD) and the intensive margin (how much: IRR 1.18), and does not vary by origin field.</p>
    <p class="code-links">Code: <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-5/evaluation-7">Host-specific or just common words?</a></p>
  </div>
</li>

<li>
  <div class="card-head"><span class="card-num">4</span><h3>Structural precursors declared dead</h3></div>
  <div class="card-body">
    <p>The pre-registered <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-4/evaluation-3">held-out test</a> returns R1_DEAD: structural precursors of sustained uptake are volume and churn correlates. Only <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-3/experiment-5">persistent-neighbour closure</a> survives (coefficient &minus;1.07, Holm p&nbsp;=&nbsp;0.015). Burt constraint is positive: emerging concepts sit in more constrained, not more brokered, ego networks.</p>
  </div>
</li>

<li>
  <div class="card-head"><span class="card-num">5</span><h3>Diffusion typology and adopter enrichment</h3></div>
  <div class="card-body">
    <p>A stable <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-3/experiment-8">two-type typology</a> (localised vs. broad from the start), an expansion-before-diffusion ordering (25 of 26 dual-onset concepts), and <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-4/evaluation-5">adopter enrichment</a> for prior partner exposure (OR 3.09; prevalence 0.79 vs.&nbsp;0.61; screen fold only).</p>
    <p class="code-links">Code: <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-4/evaluation-4">Checking concept spread types on unseen and medical data</a></p>
  </div>
</li>

</ol>
</section>

<!-- METHOD -->
<section id="method" aria-label="Method">
<h2>Method</h2>

<figure class="method-fig">
  <img src="figures/fig1_v0.jpg" alt="Study design diagram with four panels: data collection of 426 concepts and 191 MeSH concepts from 462,812 OpenAlex works; co-word network with 25 yearly snapshots of approximately 27,000 nodes; RQ1 matched event study comparing closure before sustained uptake; RQ2 host-entry grafting measuring host-vocabulary share against five-year newcomer uptake.">
  <figcaption><span class="fig-title">Figure 1. Study design and analysis pipeline.</span> (a) Data: an outcome-blind arXiv concept pool of 426 emerging scientific concepts, split into a screen fold (247) and a held-out fold (119), and an independent MeSH biomedical check population of 191 concepts. Both are drawn from 462,812 OpenAlex works. (b) Co-word network: yearly co-word snapshots (25 snapshots, ~27k nodes, ~84k edges) with Leiden communities. (c) RQ1, emergence precursors: a matched event study compares closure measures in the pre-onset window between concepts showing sustained uptake and controls. (d) RQ2, host-entry grafting: a concept enters a non-origin host subfield; the host-vocabulary share of its partner terms is the exposure in a pre-registered PPML regression predicting 5-year newcomer uptake.</figcaption>
</figure>

<p>The study assembles an outcome-blind pool of 426 scientific concepts from OpenAlex, builds yearly co-word network snapshots from 462,812 works, and tests two research questions about how new concepts establish themselves in foreign disciplinary territory.</p>

<p class="method-sub">Data</p>
<p>The <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-1/dataset-1">concept pool</a> contains 426 scientific concepts (366 emerging, 60 stationary reference) that first appeared in OpenAlex between 2005 and 2016, with 20 to 300 first-appearance papers. Of the 366 emerging concepts, 247 form the screen fold and 119 the held-out fold, split by a SHA-1 hash before any outcomes were inspected. Each concept was <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-2/experiment-1">grounded</a> through a logistic-regression classifier (F1&nbsp;=&nbsp;0.82, AUC&nbsp;=&nbsp;0.89) and variant merger (B-cubed F1&nbsp;=&nbsp;0.78). An independent check population of <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-1/dataset-3">191 new MeSH biomedical concepts</a> was drawn from MeSH descriptors established 2004 to 2018.</p>

<p class="method-sub">Co-word network</p>
<p>From a design-weighted background sample of 259,716 works, the study built 25 yearly three-year-window <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-2/experiment-3">co-occurrence snapshots</a> (approximately 27,000 nodes and 84,000 edges per snapshot) with association-strength edge weights and Leiden community detection.</p>

<p class="method-sub">RQ1: Emergence precursors</p>
<p>For each concept showing sustained uptake, a matched event study compares closure measures in the pre-onset window against a control concept from the same first-appearance band. Four closure variants are tested: general closure, turnover-residualised closure, persistent-neighbour closure (restricted to top associates present in consecutive years), and Burt constraint. Bootstrap confidence intervals and Holm-corrected p-values control for multiple testing.</p>

<p class="method-sub">RQ2: Host-entry grafting</p>
<p>A host-entry event is the first year a concept appears in a non-origin subfield together with at least five co-occurring partner terms. The host-vocabulary share is the tag-weighted mean of each partner's pre-entry publication share in the host subfield. The outcome is five-year newcomer uptake: the count of host-subfield papers by author-disjoint newcomers. The model is a Poisson pseudo-maximum-likelihood (PPML) regression with concept-clustered standard errors and two pre-registered specifications. The co-primary specification includes concept, entry-year and host fixed effects; the primary specification adds concept-by-year and host-by-year fixed effects.</p>
</section>

<!-- RESULTS -->
<section id="results" aria-label="Results">
<h2>Results</h2>

<div class="result-block">
<p class="result-label">Host-entry grafting (RQ2)</p>
<p>On the screen fold, a one-standard-deviation increase in host-vocabulary share raises newcomer uptake by 30% (co-primary IRR 1.30, 95% CI 1.16 to 1.45). On the sealed <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-4/evaluation-2">held-out fold</a>, opened once, the co-primary IRR is 1.19 (95% CI 1.06 to 1.33; the pre-declared kill rule is not triggered). On the <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-4/experiment-9">MeSH biomedical population</a>, the co-primary IRR is 1.23 (95% CI 1.12 to 1.36; verdict REPLICATED for biomedicine-to-biomedicine entries). The inverse-variance weighted pooled estimate across screen and MeSH is 1.26 (95% CI 1.17 to 1.36).</p>
<p>Co-transfer of origin companions is null across all folds and specifications. The fully saturated primary specification is inconclusive on the held-out fold (IRR 0.98, 95% CI 0.70 to 1.37, 30 clusters).</p>
</div>

<div class="result-block">
<p class="result-label">Margin decomposition</p>
<p>The host-vocabulary effect operates through both margins. The <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-5/evaluation-6">extensive-margin</a> effect is +6.4 percentage points per standard deviation (95% CI 4.8 to 8.1), approximately a 13% increase relative to the 51% base rate. The intensive-margin IRR per standard deviation is 1.18 (95% CI 1.10 to 1.27). The extensive margin accounts for 38% of the total effect (95% CI 21% to 55%); the intensive margin accounts for the remaining 62%.</p>
</div>

<div class="result-block">
<p class="result-label">Adopter enrichment</p>
<p>Newcomer scientists who adopt a concept are enriched for prior corpus exposure to its <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-4/evaluation-5">entry partners</a> (conditional logistic regression OR 3.09; prevalence 0.79 vs.&nbsp;0.61; 1,013 matched strata, screen fold only, not independently confirmed). Enrichment follows a vocabulary gradient: FOREIGN partners OR 2.88, ADJACENT partners OR 1.91, NATIVE partners OR 1.47. The design cannot separate absorptive capacity from topical proximity.</p>
</div>

<div class="result-block">
<p class="result-label">Structural precursors (RQ1)</p>
<p>Under the pre-registered kill rule, R1_DEAD: structural precursors of sustained uptake are volume and churn correlates. Only <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-3/experiment-5">persistent-neighbour closure</a> survives Holm correction on the held-out fold (panel coefficient &minus;1.07, Holm p&nbsp;=&nbsp;0.015; event-study standardised mean difference &minus;0.83, 95% CI [&minus;1.71, &minus;0.10]). General closure (Holm p&nbsp;=&nbsp;0.147) and turnover-residualised closure (Holm p&nbsp;=&nbsp;0.635) do not survive. Burt constraint is positive (+0.11, 95% CI [0.02, 0.19]): emerging concepts sit in more constrained, not more brokered, ego networks.</p>
<p>The <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-2/experiment-4">MeSH closure replication</a> is directional under a sensitivity label (standardised mean difference &minus;0.42, Holm p&nbsp;=&nbsp;0.039, n&nbsp;=&nbsp;29) but null under the primary label (&minus;0.09, Holm p&nbsp;=&nbsp;0.677, n&nbsp;=&nbsp;15).</p>
</div>

<div class="result-block">
<p class="result-label">Null findings</p>
<p>Co-transfer is null in all specifications and populations. The <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-3/experiment-6">breadth-prediction screen</a> (does openness predict how many new subfields a concept will reach?) found no effect beyond growth and level baselines. The link between pre-emergence closure and later host-entry vocabulary composition is null (partial correlation 0.025 screen, 0.053 held-out, both intervals including zero).</p>
</div>
</section>

<!-- LIMITATIONS -->
<section id="limitations" aria-label="Limitations">
<h2>Limitations</h2>
<ul class="limitations-list">

<li><span class="lim-head">Held-out fold scope.</span> The held-out fold's outcomes were sealed and opened once, but its entry events, pre-entry features and population size were computed on the same pipeline before opening. The confirmation guards against outcome-driven choices, not against every choice of frame.</li>

<li><span class="lim-head">Population bias.</span> The concept pool is dominated by physics, physical-sciences and computer-science concepts from arXiv. The MeSH population covers only biomedicine-to-biomedicine entries; its coverage rule removes 34% of partner-qualified entries. Generalisation to social sciences, humanities or engineering is untested.</li>

<li><span class="lim-head">Primary specification underpowered.</span> The fully saturated specification with concept-by-year and host-by-year fixed effects is inconclusive on the held-out fold (IRR 0.98, 30 clusters). The held-out confirmation rests on the co-primary specification, which leaves more residual variation.</li>

<li><span class="lim-head">Binary establishment null.</span> Host-vocabulary share predicts the count of newcomer papers and the probability of any newcomer uptake, but binary establishment (at least three newcomer papers in at least three of five years) is null on the held-out fold (p&nbsp;=&nbsp;0.165). The effect is graded, not threshold-based.</li>

<li><span class="lim-head">Cluster-robust inference.</span> The cluster-robust variance estimator rejects 10% to 11% of null shuffles in simulation (target 5%). Wild-cluster bootstrap and permutation tests give consistent results, but standard p-values should not be taken at face value.</li>

<li><span class="lim-head">Adopter evidence unconfirmed.</span> The adopter-level enrichment (OR 3.09) is screen-fold only, not independently confirmed. The design cannot separate absorptive capacity from topical proximity.</li>

<li><span class="lim-head">RQ1 caveats.</span> R1_DEAD under the frozen kill rule. The one confirmed row, persistent-neighbour closure, had a screen event-study interval that included zero. The held-out matching falls back to screen controls for 17 of 25 unique controls, so the estimator is not fully control-side independent.</li>

</ul>
</section>
